drills.title: Wrap a function with a log line
drills.prompt: Arrange the lines (and indent them) so the decorator prints a log line before every call of the decorated function and still returns the function's result. Two lines do not belong.
drills.explain: A decorator is a function that takes a function (func), defines an inner wrapper that adds behaviour around the call, and returns the wrapper itself. The line @log_call above def brew means brew = log_call(brew), so the decorator must be defined first. return wrapper hands back the function; return wrapper() would call it right away. @log_call() would call log_call with no function, which is the pattern for decorators with arguments, not this one.

drills.title: Pause and resume a generator
drills.prompt: Fill the three blanks so countdown becomes a generator that hands out one number per request, then ask it for two numbers by hand.
drills.explain: yield hands out a value and pauses the function right there; the next request resumes after the yield with n still remembered. next(gen) is that request, so the first two calls give 3 and 2. A generator can be used only once and keeps its place, so list(gen) collects what is left: [1]. return would end the function at the first number and make a normal function, not a generator.

drills.title: What did the decorator do to the name?
drills.prompt: Read the code and type exactly what it prints, one line per line of output.
drills.explain: Both decorators return the result of the original function, so the calls print chai and served. The name is different: @plain replaces brew by the inner function called wrapper, so brew.__name__ is wrapper. functools.wraps copies the name (and docstring) of the original onto the wrapper, so serve keeps its name. Lost names make logs and error messages hard to read.

drills.title: A generator that is not one
drills.prompt: The program stops with a TypeError instead of printing the countdown list. Click the line that causes it, then choose the right fix.
drills.explain: return ends the function at the first number and gives back a plain int, so list() cannot loop over it (TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable). yield makes countdown a generator: it hands out 3, pauses, and resumes after the yield to hand out 2 and 1. A generator yields values one at a time; it does not return a list. yield from needs something iterable, not a single number.

drills.title: Review the AI's retry decorator
drills.prompt: An AI assistant wrote this retry decorator. It runs, but tick the statements that point at real problems.

issues.text: wrapper is not decorated with functools.wraps, so the function loses its name (the import is unused)
issues.why: The program prints wrapper instead of flaky_download. Debugging, logs and frameworks that read __name__ or the docstring all see the wrong function. Add @functools.wraps(func) above def wrapper.

issues.text: When every attempt fails the decorator returns None without any error
issues.why: always_down() prints None, so the caller cannot tell a failed download from a function that returns nothing. After the last attempt the original exception should be raised again (and attempts could be logged).

non_issues.text: Three nested functions are too many; retry(times) should take func directly
non_issues.why: A decorator that takes its own argument needs one extra level: retry(times) returns decorator, which takes func and returns wrapper. That is why @retry(3) is written with brackets.
They let the wrapper accept and pass on whatever arguments the decorated function takes, so one decorator works for any function.

non_issues.text: range(times) runs one attempt too few or too many
non_issues.why: range(3) gives 3 values, so the function is tried at most 3 times, as @retry(3) promises. The unused loop variable attempt is harmless (it is often written _).

drills.explain: When you review a decorator, check what happens to the result, the name and the errors. This one keeps the result but loses the name and hides the final failure. The nesting and *args, **kwargs are the normal shape of a decorator with an argument.
